title: Scaling Certifiable Safety for Embodied AI: From Fixed Domains toward Open-World Autonomy

rawEventDetails: Speaker Duy Phuong Nguyen Details Event Description Robots are being deployed faster and closer to humans, making safety increasingly difficult to quantify and certify. Analytical methods often rely on reduced-order models, whereas numerical methods can provide stronger guarantees but quickly become intractable. Learning scales to high-dimensional systems, yet typically offers only empirical or probabilistic assurances. This dissertation combines the scalability of learning with the rigor of control-theoretic safety. In the first part, we develop certifiable safety filters for a designed world with a fixed Operational Design Domain (ODD), which specifies the admissible dynamics, environmental conditions, disturbances, and failure modes. Safety synthesis is formulated as solving a zero-sum game between the robot and an adversary representing the admissible disturbances. We develop a provably convergent adversarial actor–critic method to approximate the game solution and synthesize neural safety policies for high-dimensional systems. This framework enables full-order safety-filter synthesis and zero-shot deployment across different high-dimensional robotic systems. The learned safety value function can also serve as a state–action control barrier function, recovering the maximal robust safety envelope while minimally modifying the task policy. We further show that sufficiently permissive filtering does not degrade asymptotic performance, enabling reinforcement learning that reaches state-of-the-art performance faster than imperfectly safe methods, with zero violations under a perfect filter. Finally, we show that goal-conditioned reach-avoid safety filters make interventions preserve the task rather than only avoid failure, and expand rather than restrict what robots can safely do, from quadruped parkour to underactuated industrial cranes. The second part extends safety beyond the designed world, where the ODD can no longer be held fixed. We first introduce dynamic ODDs, which condition safety values and policies on operating limits inferred and updated at runtime, allowing the robot to adapt as physical conditions change. However, this is not enough when the relevant hazards and failure modes were never specified in advance. We therefore develop an open-context architecture in which generative models interpret the scene, revise the relevant ODD, and select control-grounded safety tools through a representation shared with classical autonomy. This progression lays the foundation for extending certifiable safety from fixed physical envelopes toward open, human-centered autonomy. An embargo has been approved for this thesis. To view a copy of the thesis please stop by the EQUAD Graduate office B209. Adviser: Jaime Fernández Fisac
summaryRaw: Scaling Certifiable Safety for Embodied AI: From Fixed Domains toward Open-World Autonomy

rawEventDetails: Speaker Sarita Adve Affiliation University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Details Event Description Abstract: Immersive computing, including virtual, augmented, and mixed reality (collectively, extended reality or XR), integrates the virtual with the physical. Immersive systems enable AI to escape from the chatbot on a 2D screen into the 3D world around us, where it can perceive, understand, and act alongside the people who live and work there. AI, in turn, is making immersive systems more capable. We refer to the convergence of immersive computing and AI as immersive intelligence. Immersive intelligence places demands on computer systems that are orders of magnitude beyond what current systems deliver: real-time inference over many interacting models, within the power envelope of all-day wearable devices, with quality ultimately judged by the human experience. Meeting these demands requires distributing immersive intelligence across the wearable, nearby devices, the edge, and the datacenter, and evaluating the resulting designs with new human-centric metrics. I will discuss recent work and what it suggests about the architecture of these systems, from the wearable to the datacenter, and about the opportunities ahead for the architecture and systems community. The talk will draw on ILLIXR, our open-source end-to-end XR system testbed, which supports distributed XR and first-of-their-kind AI-enabled XR capabilities, and on the IMMERSE Center for Immersive Computing at Illinois, which brings together research on immersive technologies, applications, and human experience. Bio: Sarita Adve is the Richard T. Cheng Professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her research interests span the system stack, from hardware to applications, with a current focus on immersive intelligence. She directs the IMMERSE Center for Immersive Computing, which brings together expertise in immersive technologies, applications, and human experience to perform research, educate a new workforce, and build infrastructure to enable a new era of immersive computing. Her group released ILLIXR (Illinois Extended Reality testbed), an open-source end-to-end extended reality (XR) system and research testbed that is used widely. She led the XR section of SRC's MAPT 2.0 roadmap for the semiconductor industry. Her early work on data-race-free memory consistency models and later work on the memory models for the Java and C++ programming languages form the foundation for memory models used in most hardware and software systems today. She is also known for her work on heterogeneous architectures and software-driven hardware resiliency. She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a fellow of the ACM, IEEE, and AAAS. She has received several awards, including the ACM/IEEE-CS Ken Kennedy award, the ACM SIGARCH Maurice Wilkes award, and the ACM SIGARCH Alan D. Berenbaum Distinguished Service award. As ACM SIGARCH chair, she co-founded the CARES movement, winner of the CRA distinguished service award, to address discrimination and harassment in computer science research events. She received her PhD from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and her B.Tech. from the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

title: Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design for Programmable Sensor-Fusion Perception and Scalable In-Memory Computing
series: Final Public Oral Examinations,Final Public Orals
content: Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. rawEventDetails: Speaker Rakshit Pathak Details Event Description Machine-perception systems are increasingly deployed at the edge, where they must combine remote sensing (e.g., vision, lidar) with embedded point sensing (e.g., inertial, acoustic, locationing) under tightly constrained energy budgets. Exploiting both forms of sensing requires fusion algorithms that generalize across modalities and tasks, as well as computing platforms that can execute them with high energy efficiency while retaining programmability. This dissertation addresses these needs through algorithm-hardware co-design, spanning the fusion model, processor architecture, silicon prototypes and system infrastructure. First, a generalized Deep-Learning Sensor-Fusion (DL-SF) model is developed, which projects embedded-sensor features into sparse two-dimensional feature maps via domain transformation, scales them to the receptive field of each layer, and concatenates them throughout a convolutional backbone. Across four bookend applications (depth-map generation, 3D human-pose estimation, human trajectory forecasting and human-activity recognition), the DL-SF model improves accuracy and sample efficiency relative to vision-only, early-fusion and late-fusion baselines, for example requiring 3,680 rather than 16k training samples to reach iso-accuracy (98.2%) in activity recognition. Second, the computational structure of the DL-SF model is analyzed to drive the design of a heterogeneous processor in 28nm CMOS, integrating a RISC-V CPU with ISA extensions for embedded-sensor feature extraction, an NVDLA-based convolution accelerator, a Q22.10 fixed-point domain transformation unit, and a memory-data densifier for dense/sparse activation referencing. The prototype executes all four applications end-to-end with 9.3 to 28.1× lower energy and 300 to 500× lower latency than software execution on the CPU, and 15.6 to 24.6× lower energy than reference GPU implementations. Third, this dissertation develops the host-to-chip system infrastructure for a scalable in-memory-computing (IMC) neural-network accelerator in 16nm CMOS, comprising a 4×4 array of IMC cores connected by an on-chip network. This includes the chip interface connecting off-chip signals through the activation and weight buffers to the on-chip network, a PCIe-based FPGA controller using the RIFFA framework, an FPGA emulator of the IMC core for pre-silicon software validation, and a C library that bridges Python-level neural-network mapping tools to the hardware. This infrastructure enabled the measurement and demonstration of CIFAR-10 and ImageNet networks on the prototype. Adviser: Naveen Verma
summaryRaw: Algorithm-Hardware Co-Design for Programmable Sensor-Fusion Perception and Scalable In-Memory Computing

rawEventDetails: Speaker Kyle Frohna Affiliation Stanford Energy Postdoctoral Fellow, Physics PhD Details Event Description Abstract: Growing electricity demands and climate targets are forcing unprecedented restructuring of our electrical grid. Solving these issues requires increasing renewable energy generation and storage capacity at exponential rates. To achieve this, we must rapidly improve existing technologies while discovering and optimising new materials and devices at unprecedented speed to ensure diverse, secure energy supply with resilient, domestic supply chains. However, unlike incumbent semiconductors, next-generation energy devices are highly disordered on multiple length scales, and this has massive implications for their operating principles, performance and stability. Understanding and improving these devices requires high resolution and throughput characterisation of this multiscale disorder. In this presentation, I will describe the development of multimodal microscopy toolkits sensitive to optoelectronic and electrochemical activity, crystal structure, and chemical composition. I will then detail their application to materials relevant for renewable energy generation and storage. Using halide perovskite semiconductors as a highly disordered model system, I will discuss the origins of their remarkable tolerance to extremely high concentrations of defects, the chemical and structural origins of this disorder, and how this disorder is predictive of solar cell performance and degradation. Then, in a range of rechargeable battery chemistries, I will show, with single particle resolution, how disorder can seed capacity loss and irreversible degradation, but can also unlock exciting new applications. I will highlight disorder as both a unifying challenge and design axis across a range of crucial technologies. Bio: Kyle Frohna is a Stanford Energy Postdoctoral Fellow in the Departments of Materials Science & Engineering and Electrical Engineering working with Professors William Chueh and Daniel Congreve where he develops tools to study batteries under operational conditions. He completed his PhD in Physics and an EPSRC Doctoral Prize Postdoctoral Fellowship at the Cavendish Laboratory, University of Cambridge in the group of Professor Sam Stranks studying halide perovskite materials and solar cells at the nanoscale and received the Woodruff PhD Thesis Prize from the Institute of Physics. He received his B.Sc. in Nanoscience: The Physics and Chemistry of Advanced Materials from Trinity College Dublin, Ireland, close to where he grew up. His research focuses on how to characterise, understand and manipulate disorder to improve next-generation energy materials with a latest thrust on coupling high-throughput experimentation with advanced characterisation. His work has been recognised with awards including the Cambridge Trust Scholarship, Schiff Foundation Studentship, Robert Gardiner Scholarship and the Winton Sustainability Fellowship. Outside of research, he is an avid heavy metal drummer and likes to practice olympic weightlifting. Sponsor Dane de Quilettes Contact Patricia Kuczmarski [email protected]

title: Information Technologies at the Fundamental Physical Limits
content: Abstract Fundamental physical laws set the performance limits of computing, communications, and sensing. Advances in nanotechnology and integrated circuits have brought these technologies closer to their classical limits, while quantum resources offer ways to extend their performance. rawEventDetails: Speaker Volkan Gurses Affiliation MIT Details Event Description Abstract Fundamental physical laws set the performance limits of computing, communications, and sensing. Advances in nanotechnology and integrated circuits have brought these technologies closer to their classical limits, while quantum resources offer ways to extend their performance. In this talk, I will discuss the physical and information-theoretic bounds that govern these systems and present large-scale integrated systems in silicon photonics and electronics designed to approach them. The talk will cover experimental demonstrations and proposed architectures across three areas: quantum computing on CMOS and hybrid classical–quantum computing; quantum coherent transceivers that encode information in non-classical light, with a path beyond the Shannon limit toward the Holevo limit; and quantum phased arrays and squeezed-light sensors for sensing beyond the standard quantum limit toward the Heisenberg limit. For each system, I will connect the underlying theory to integrated circuit design, experimental results, and applications. I will conclude with a path toward scalable, deployable technologies within today’s CMOS infrastructure. Bio Volkan Gurses is a postdoctoral researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a lecturer at the California Institute of Technology, and a visiting researcher at NVIDIA Research. He received his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering with a subject minor in Physics and his M.S. in Electrical Engineering from the California Institute of Technology, and his B.S. in Electrical Engineering with Research Option from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His research is broadly on integrated systems, with a focus on studying the fundamental physical and information-theoretic limits of technologies (e.g., Landauer, Holevo, Heisenberg) and developing integrated systems that can operate at these limits. During his Ph.D., he founded a chip design startup named Foundation Silicon after winning the Caltech Entrepreneurship Prize. He was additionally awarded the Carver Mead New Adventures Fund, R. David Middlebrook Fellowship, Caltech EAS Division Fellowship, Tau Beta Pi Fellowship, IEEE MTT-S Undergraduate/Pre-Graduate Scholarship, European Union Contest for Young Scientists CERN Special Donated Prize, and First Prize in the Turkish National Research Contest, and he was named a Rising Star by Cell Press. Sponsor Electrical & Computer Engineering

rawEventDetails: Details Event Description Abstract: Progress in solid-state electronics has been driven by increasingly precise control over electrons, atoms, and interfaces. From controlled doping to high-κ/metal-gate stacks and gate-all-around nanosheets, each generation of silicon CMOS technology has depended on engineering matter at the scale of a few atoms. Superconducting quantum computing rests on a similar foundation: the nonlinearity that defines a qubit comes from a Josephson junction whose tunnel barrier is an amorphous oxide about one nanometer thick. For future computing, from energy-efficient AI hardware to scalable quantum processors, a key challenge is to extend atomic-scale control to new materials and interfaces without sacrificing wafer-scale manufacturability. In this talk, I will introduce physical principles that allow atomic precision and wafer-scale manufacturing to coexist for emerging electronic and quantum technologies. First, I will present surface-kinetics-controlled synthesis of an air-stable monolayer superconductor at the inch scale, which reaches a kinetic inductance of ~0.7 nH/sq in superconducting circuits, together with atomically thin n-type and p-type semiconductors for CMOS applications. Second, I will discuss electrostatic-force-enabled transfer and heterogenous integration of these materials onto functional electronic and superconducting circuits with clean, minimally damaged interfaces. Finally, I will show how nano-scale strain modulates the band structures in ultra-scaled 2D transistors, delivering on-currents above 1 mA/µm at 1 V with CMOS-compatible contacts. These studies, spanning material synthesis, interface formation, and device engineering, demonstrate that atomic precision can be achieved at wafer scale and open new opportunities for energy-efficient electronics and scalable quantum technologies. Sponsor Host: Professor Nathalie de Leon, ECE

content: Abstract: Computers are increasingly integrated into embodied systems that operate in complex real-world environments, such as autonomous robots and smart wearable/Extended Reality (XR) glasses. rawEventDetails: Speaker Yuhao Zhu Affiliation University of Rochester Details Event Description Abstract: Computers are increasingly integrated into embodied systems that operate in complex real-world environments, such as autonomous robots and smart wearable/Extended Reality (XR) glasses. These systems must continuously sense and interpret the physical world while also generating information that engages human perceptual and cognitive systems. This talk argues that programming and architecting future computer systems must integrate sensing and human cognition into the computing stack, and presents my lab’s work toward this vision. First, I will discuss the co-design of sensing and computation, where we design novel computational image sensors and compile visual programs across heterogeneous sensing and computing hardware. Second, I will discuss co-optimizing computing with humans, where we build novel computational models of human visual perception that provide perceptual, not numerical, specifications and constraints for navigating the enormous design space of visual programs. Together, these projects point toward an exciting future of computing that jointly reasons about machines, the physical world, and human cognition. Bio: Yuhao Zhu is an Associate Professor of Computer Science, Brain and Cognitive Sciences, and an Asaro Biggar Family Fellow in Data Science, all at University of Rochester, where he and his students are mostly drawn to research problems at the intersection of computer architecture, sensing, and human factors. With his collaborators and students, he has won multiple IEEE Micro Top Picks in Computer Architecture for "novelty and potential for long-term impact," along with best paper awards/nominations at MICRO, HPCA, ASPLOS, and IEEE VR. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

rawEventDetails: Speaker Anant Kale Affiliation Harvard Details Event Description Abstract: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter is a promising probe of fundamental physics while also being practically useful in making progress on long-standing problems in condensed matter. A paradigmatic example is understanding the physics of high-Tc cuprate materials, where many open questions remain regarding the origin and nature of unconventional superconductivity, pseudogap phase, and spin and charge stripes. Ultracold fermionic atoms in optical lattices provide a clean and controllable realization of the Fermi-Hubbard model, believed to capture the essential physics of the cuprates. In this talk, I will describe our recent experimental results achieving a several-fold reduction in temperature, reaching a regime inaccessible to numerical simulation. Using equilibrium and dynamical probes, we experimentally characterize the pseudogap phase, thought to be a parent state for the d-wave superconductor. In the pseudogap regime, we observe novel peaks versus doping in the compressibility and nematic susceptibility, possible precursors to charge and spin stripes. We also observe direct signatures of spin stripes at the lowest temperatures, although these appear to differ from the conventional picture of stripes. Finally, I will describe ongoing efforts to push beyond the plain Hubbard model, including a three-band Lieb lattice and next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′, which may play an important role in understanding the long-sought-after high-Tc superconductivity. Sponsor Host: Professor Jeff Thompson, ECE

title: From Scalable Systems to Quantum Computing: Emerging Applications and Computing Challenges
content: Abstract: Over the past several decades, the high performance computing (HPC) community has played a central role in advancing computing infrastructures, from operating systems to cloud platforms and large-scale distributed environments. rawEventDetails: Speaker Dilma Da Silva Affiliation Texas A&M University Details Event Description Abstract: Over the past several decades, the high performance computing (HPC) community has played a central role in advancing computing infrastructures, from operating systems to cloud platforms and large-scale distributed environments. Many of the systems challenges addressed by this community are now reappearing in the context of emerging scientific workflows that combine advances in artificial intelligence (AI), HPC, and quantum computing. This talk connects a long-standing research trajectory in scalable systems with more recent work in quantum computing. It discusses emerging opportunities for quantum computing in scientific simulation and optimization, with applications in chemistry, materials science, geosciences & energy, illustrating the distinction between promising demonstrations and practical computational advantages. The talk will explore how expertise in HPC and distributed systems can help address the challenges of turning promising quantum computing capabilities into practical applications. As quantum technologies evolve toward larger and more programmable platforms, challenges involving hybrid quantum–classical workflow orchestration, runtime and compilation systems, resource management, distributed control, and reliability are becoming increasingly important. We will discuss how familiar systems abstractions and techniques can contribute to the emerging quantum software stack and enable the integration of quantum resources into scientific computing environments. The presentation will conclude with a brief overview of the evolving U.S. federal research funding landscape in quantum computing, quantum networking, and quantum sensing. Bio: Dilma Da Silva is a Regents Professor and holder of the Ford Design Professorship II in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Texas A&M University. From July 2022 to June 2026, she served in several leadership positions at the U.S. National Science Foundation. Her roles at Texas A&M include Department Head (2014-2019), Associate Dean (2019-2020), interim Director of the Texas A&M Institute of Data Science, and interim Director of the Texas A&M Cybersecurity Center. Her primary research interests are high performance computing, computer science education, and quantum computing. Before joining Texas A&M, she worked at Qualcomm Research (2012-2014), IBM Research (2000-2012), and the University of São Paulo (1996-2000). Dilma is an ACM Distinguished Scientist. She received her doctoral degree in computer science from Georgia Tech in 1997 and her bachelor's and master's degrees from the University of São Paulo, Brazil. She is passionate about mentoring and supporting the next generation of computing researchers and practitioners. Sponsor Emerging Frontiers in Computer Architecture and Systems

title: High-Frequency Power Electronics for Semiconductor Plasma Processing
content: Abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) plasmas enable critical etching and deposition processes in semiconductor manufacturing. rawEventDetails: Speaker Alex Jurkov Affiliation MKS Details Event Description Abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) plasmas enable critical etching and deposition processes in semiconductor manufacturing. As device structures become increasingly three-dimensional and feature dimensions shrink, these processes demand tighter control of RF power over wide operating ranges and during rapid changes in plasma impedance. Meeting these requirements presents a central challenge for high-frequency power electronics: achieving high efficiency together with wide-range power control and fast dynamic response. This talk explores how coordinated design of RF inverters, power-combining networks, and tunable matching networks can address this challenge. Following a brief introduction to semiconductor plasma processing and its power-delivery requirements, this presentation examines soft-switched inverters that accommodate variable loading, power-combining architectures that enable rapid and efficient output-power control, and phase-switched impedance modulation (PSIM) for high-speed impedance matching. Experimental examples include a 13.56 MHz RF power system operating over a 5 W–5 kW range with microsecond pulsing capability, and a 3.5 kW tunable matching network for dynamic plasma loads. The talk will conclude with open research opportunities in adaptive RF power architectures, high-frequency components, sensing, and control. Bio: Alex Jurkov received the B.Sc. degree in Electrical Engineering and Computer Engineering from the University of Calgary, Calgary, AB, Canada, and the S.M. and Ph.D. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Cambridge, MA. Since 2019, he has been a Senior Principal Scientist in the Advanced Development Group at MKS Instruments, Rochester, NY, where he leads research on next-generation RF power delivery systems for plasma processing. He is also a Visiting Research Scientist at MIT’s Laboratory for Electromagnetic and Electronic Systems. His research interests include high-efficiency RF power converters, phase-switched impedance modulation (PSIM), high-bandwidth tunable matching networks, and embedded mixed-signal control systems for semiconductor manufacturing. Sponsor Professor Minjie Chen
